detail.longDescription: It seems to me the industry is at a divergence point, with strong forces pull in opposite directions. In the "developers are team leads / checkpoint verifiers" corner we have: - Microsoft, re "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product" (Nadella) and "become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work" <https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/18/microsoft-ceo-satya-nadella-explains-why-he-asked-60k-employees-to-quit/> -- Microsoft has always championed "AI as a team member", even as a product. - Salesforce <https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/how-engineering-became-agentic/> - Stripe <https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents> - Uber, Shopify, Spotify, Meta In the "developers use harnesses to improve personal velocity and quality corner we have: - Netflix <https://qconsf.com/presentation/nov2026/how-netflix-retrofitted-its-sdlc-ai-coding-agents> - Amazon <https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/amazon-software-engineer-role-guideline-ai> - ... Google, but it's hard to find more than anecdotal references These two approaches, in my view, are not compatible. Fully, or even just semi-automated feature factories keep the context, leaving the developer to validate artifacts and manage the flow, shifting responsibility to specs and building automated verifiers. It lets less technical people into the product development loop but keeps the code an AI-only territory. On the other hand, a harness keeps the developer in control, but sacrifices velocity and requires higher technical prowess, or at least understanding, of what's being generated. Which way is the industry going to go? Are AI-only maintained code bases going to collapse under their own weight? Are "technical" developers going to be sidelined for higher delivery velocity? Will we see two types of businesses - features and infra, each taking a polar position in this? Or even within the same business, different teams?
